The simmering resentment had been building for years. Mark felt consistently overlooked at work, consistently passed over for promotions in favor of David, who seemed to effortlessly charm their boss, Ms. Evans. Mark convinced himself David wasn't *better*, just *better at appearing* better. He’d started to view David’s successes not as achievements, but as intentional sabotage of his own career.

This perceived injustice warped Mark's thinking. He began obsessively documenting David's actions, searching for anything he could spin into a negative. A casual joke David made at a team lunch? Mark reinterpreted it as a belittling comment directed at a client. A slight delay in responding to an email? Mark painted it as deliberate negligence, showcasing David's unreliability. He carefully crafted these instances into a narrative of incompetence and unprofessional conduct.

He didn't approach Ms. Evans directly with concrete evidence of wrongdoing – there *was* no actual wrongdoing. Instead, he subtly seeded doubt. "I'm just a little concerned about some things I've noticed with David's approach to the Peterson account," he'd say, vaguely alluding to the misinterpreted lunch comment.  Or, "I wonder if David fully understood the urgency with the Miller report, given the delay in his reply," hinting at the email issue. He framed these as expressions of *concern for the company*, not attacks on David.

The strategy worked, disturbingly well. Ms. Evans, initially dismissive, began to ask David pointed questions, challenging his judgment, and requiring increased oversight. David, confused and frustrated, began to falter under the pressure. His confidence eroded, and his performance *did* suffer – not because of any initial flaw, but because he was constantly second-guessing himself and navigating a hostile work environment subtly created by Mark's manipulations.  Mark, watching David struggle, felt a twisted sense of satisfaction. He’d “evened the score,” though at the cost of a colleague's well-being and the company's overall morale.  He believed he'd won, but he hadn't. He'd simply created a corrosive atmosphere of mistrust and damage.
